Own simulation (not a published source): count caps of 5 to 50 changed regret by at most about 0.15 at 30 to 60 pulls, even after a mid-run switch.

Separately, demonstration choice matters: one query-correct demo can beat using all demos (Chen et al.).

fix: More facts attached to one cue slows recognition in people, and usually lowers accuracy mainly through extra false alarms (hit-rate effects are mixed). This holds for fictional facts and real-world knowledge; in a Dutch conference poster with semantically similar concepts RT rose with fan in both experiments but accuracy fell only in the repeated-concept experiment (similar-concept accuracy near ceiling).

problem: Cao et al. numbers verified (0.991 to 0.915 at list size 32; GPT-4 d' about 4.1 to 3.1) but the paper does not call the effect small (d' drop about 1.0, versus about 1.2 in humans); and Roberts et al. found no fan effect for GPT-2/Llama-2/RoBERTa only in the pretraining-fan experiment, while the in-context experiment tested only Mistral and SOLAR, so 'when all facts are in context ... not GPT-2, Llama-2' is not supported.

In token probabilities, Roberts et al. found human-like fan effects for Mistral and SOLAR but not RoBERTa, GPT-2 or Llama-2 (pretraining fan; Llama-3 weak and non-significant); their in-context fan test covered only Mistral and SOLAR.

problem: Wang and Sun's abstract says accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero (3 to 400 updates, models from 0.6B to 637B across Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Meta, Nvidia) but the figure caption says only 'most models' showed a quasi-log-linear drop, with exceptions and two-phase declines, and Chattaraj and Raj (39 models) describe proactive interference as collapsing bimodally at high interference and do not state a log-linear fit; the '35 to 39 models' merges two separate studies built on the same task design.
fix: In Wang and Sun's PI-LLM task (46 keys, 3 to 400 updates per key, about 35 models from 0.6B to 637B parameters across many labs), accuracy at reading the latest value of a key falls approximately log-linearly toward zero for most models, with some exceptions and two-phase declines. A follow-up with 39 models (Chattaraj and Raj) confirms that proactive interference is severe in every model, but describes its collapse as bimodal at high interference rather than log-linear.

problem: Hedged ('may') and supported: LearnLab stoichiometry (no learning effect, about 21 percent less time), Min et al. problem: BACON.3 order effects and AI-Newton simple-before-complex are confirmed (Ohm 4593 productions is a cross-law cost, not an order effect), but STAHL only takes an ordered list and its examples are ordered historically; the paper does not say it needs historical order.
fix: Order and incrementality matter for cost and for reuse: BACON.3 reached the same law whatever the data order but with different computation (productions fired ranged from 1119 to 4593 across laws, Ohm highest); STAHL processes reactions as an ordered list, fed in historical order in its examples, and builds on models inferred earlier; AI-Newton discovers simple concepts (mass) before more complex ones (force) and reuses them across experiments.

problem: ABACUS (subsets with logic-style preconditions) and BACON.1 (never rejects a hypothesis; cannot formulate conditional laws) are confirmed, but none of the listed sources says sums and differences are much harder than products and ratios; ABACUS only generates sum/difference terms under units constraints.
fix: Laws need scope conditions: ABACUS learns separate equations for data subsets and derives logic-style conditions stating when each applies; BACON.1 never rejects a hypothesis once formed and cannot formulate conditional laws.

problem: Numbers confirmed (Staal g=0.20 across all tools, Prakash 0.38 for guided reflection only; 62% written-case and 31% visual tasks, 7% patients), but none of the opened sources states that many trials come from one lab network, and the 0.20 to 0.38 range mixes two different pools (all workplace tools versus guided reflection).
fix: A structured second look at a held diagnosis (list findings for, against, expected-but-missing, then alternatives) raises human diagnostic accuracy by a small to moderate amount: Hedges g 0.20 across all workplace reasoning tools (29 studies) and effect size 0.38 for guided reflection specifically (44-study review). Most trials used written cases (62%) or visual tasks (31%); only 2 of 29 used real or standardised patients.

problem: Numbers confirmed (44.5 vs 45.0, N=204; CFS N=191), but the two trials are from the same McMaster group (Sherbino and Norman on both), and Sibbald and de Bruin 2012 found analytic instructions improved ECG re-reading scores (F=15, p<0.0001), contradicting the blanket claim.
fix: In two trials from one research group, general instructions to be slow, careful and reflective did not raise diagnostic accuracy in residents (44.5 vs 45.0 percent, N=204) and cognitive forcing strategy training did not reduce bias errors in students (N=191); however, in one ECG study instructing residents to use an analytic strategy on re-reading did improve scores, so the evidence on plain instructions is mixed.

problem: Kaemmer 2021 supports 0.75 vs 0.49 (0.43 for the checklist without the answer is not visible in the abstract, only that it did not improve), but 'only when' generalises from one 90-student experiment; the review (Mamede and Schmidt) only says content-focused checklists appear to help, and Sibbald 2013 is a generic checklist.
fix: In one randomised experiment (90 advanced students), a 17-item differential diagnosis checklist raised accuracy from 0.49 (control) to 0.75 when it contained the correct diagnosis, while a checklist lacking it did not improve accuracy and might slightly reduce it; reviews suggest content-focused checklists help more than process-focused ones.

problem: In Mamede 2019 only cued reflection beat free reflection (p<0.02); modelled reflection did not differ from free (p>0.05). The p<.001 and the worked-example result are from Fernandes 2021, which used worked examples, not 'faded' examples, and reports no expertise-reversal finding.
fix: Guidance beats free reflection: cued reflection beat free reflection in novices (0.58 vs 0.41, p<0.02; modelled reflection did not differ from free reflection), and an independent group found that cued reflection and worked examples both beat free reflection (p<.001) in third- and sixth-year students, with no difference between cued and worked example.

problem: Minor: the reflection-and-calibration result is a single N=61 study; the eye-tracking study (N=19) did not test reflection, only that confidence (64-67%) did not track accuracy.

Liu et al. Table (CommonsenseQA) gives GPT-4 84.11 to 73.55 under the error-presuming prompt (a 10.6-point drop); 66.34 is the GPT-3.5 figure under that prompt. All other numbers (Huang et al. Table 3, oracle, SCoRe 15.8/4.6) match.
fix: Intrinsic LLM self-correction without an outside signal lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after five calls); earlier gains came from oracle labels deciding when to stop (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 with oracle). The sign depends on the prompt: a prompt that presumes an error cost GPT-4 about 10.6 points on CommonsenseQA (84.11 to 73.55; GPT-3.5 fell 75.92 to 66.34) while a neutral prompt left GPT-4 at 84.60; an untreated Gemini 1.0 Pro changed 15.8 percent of right MATH answers to wrong and 4.6 percent of wrong to right.

problem: Minor: the study calls the MedQA result a modest gain, and m1 is a fine-tuned 7B/32B model, so 'reasoning models in medicine' is a slight widening.
Minor: 55.9 to 71.4 is CoVe factor+revise against a few-shot baseline (factored alone is 63.7); other numbers match and DERA open-ended MedQA stayed about 70%.

Zhang 2025 (MAD wins at most about 15% of 36 settings against CoT), Wang 2024 and Tran 2026 support the claim, but Wunderlich 2026 (cited for CoT 64.3, SC 68.7) found same-model debate (70.0) beat self-consistency (68.7) at comparable compute and recommends multi-agent over single-agent, so 'same-model debate usually loses to sampling and voting' is contested; MoA there is not clearly different-model mixing.
fix: At matched budgets, self-refinement usually does worse than sampling more first passes and voting, and several studies find multi-agent debate rarely beats chain of thought (no MAD method won more than about 15 percent of 36 settings against CoT) and loses to self-consistency, but results conflict: on MMLU-Pro (CoT 64.3, SC 68.7, self-refinement below CoT) one study found debate (70.0) and mixture-of-agents (71.4) beat self-consistency at comparable compute, and single-agent matched or beat multi-agent at equal thinking tokens on multi-hop QA.

fix: Reviews list 28 intervention studies on dual-process reasoning interventions (existing studies largely limited to early-career doctors, with heterogeneous measures), and only 13 of 87 health debiasing studies targeted health professionals, with transfer to real-life settings named as a main challenge.

Flyvbjerg et al. state the HK schedule overrun difference (+58% vs +38%) is not statistically significant (p=0.089; only the share of late projects differs, p=0.048); Hsieh's prompt lists weighted/trimmed mean or median, not only a plain average; the Lovallo-Clarke-Camerer field test is not among the opened sources.
fix: Local classes can differ from global ones (HK road cost overrun +11% vs benchmark +20%; HK schedule overrun +58% vs +38% but that mean difference is not significant, though the share of late projects was higher, 8 in 10 vs 6 in 10). Class choice is the weak point and Kahneman and Lovallo only advise trying both classes; no opened source gives a rule for resolving disagreeing classes. In LLM work the Hsieh example simply averages three estimates (30, 35, 40 to 35%) and its prompt suggests a weighted or trimmed mean or median.

problem: Opened Parsons, PMC ethnography, Feast, Hu, Storm and Maher-Tang abstract pages; all small qualitative or protocol studies as described. Absence claim (no rival-model test) not testable from sources, and Cash et al. 2023 is a quantitative reanalysis but not a rival-model test.

The Halstrom and Galle abstract only says co-evolution has merit but leaves practitioners without guidance; the full-text statement that it is not defining and does not always occur could not be retrieved (PDF download truncated twice); Cross's chapter says the model's general validity is confirmed, with direction not fixed.
fix: Co-evolution of problem and solution is widely treated as a valid model of design (Cross: general validity confirmed in nine-designer protocol data), but its direction is not fixed (the solution space may be structured before the problem space), and Halstrom and Galle argue it leaves practitioners without guidance; the claim that it is not defining or does not always occur is not shown in the sources opened.

problem: Only Parsons and Shukla (n=11, qualitative vignettes) opened and it supports solution-side triggers (tool limits, time pressure, abandoned chart designs); the second listed source (Applied Sciences 2020) returned Access Denied, its evidence lines show new problem entities followed solution work only overall and reversed in ideation, and Parsons is listed twice; Cash et al. 2023 links transitions to uncertainty, not solution-side events. 'Mostly' is not shown by any quantified count.
fix: In a qualitative study of 11 expert visualization designers (Parsons and Shukla 2025), reframing was often prompted by solution-side events such as tool limits, time pressure and abandoned chart designs that failed to convey the message, not only by a planned problem-framing step; a quantitative protocol study of student teams found this only overall and reversed during ideation.

problem: Gigerenzer-Hoffrage 50% vs 28% (short menu) not directly seen; Barbey-Sloman confirms 46% vs 16%. Opened BBS review (51%, 31%, physicians 10 to 46), PMC9903474 (34% to 68%, 577 students; results text says 36% in places) and PMC11980142 (chaining 10.6%/4.9%).

The 'estimated seen base rates accurately but did not use them' result is one simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner et al.) reported in the Griffin-Koehler-Brenner commentary; a19 and a20 are the same PDF, and Bruckmaier et al. (2021) says nothing about base-rate use; 'causal' as a shrinking condition is not supported in the opened text (BBS only notes causal base-rate problems differ).
fix: In a simulated stock-market learning paradigm (Brenner and colleagues, reported in Griffin, Koehler and Brenner's commentary), participants estimated the base rates they had experienced accurately but their probability judgments were largely unaffected by them; base-rate use rises with counting or natural-frequency procedures and when the problem makes nested set structure transparent (Barbey and Sloman 2007).

(66.4 to 73.2, 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66, errors fixed up to ~40% and new errors max ~12%); the second listed source (Self-Discover) is a different method and does not corroborate, so the claim rests on one paper (Google, no independent replication).

Hackathon result matches Egea et al. (second of six, abandoned concepts on minor difficulties, fixation); for O'Hara only the abstract-level solution-jumping description was reachable (techrxiv blocked), so the 100% detection of 6 seeded mismatches and about 0.01 USD per session could not be verified, and 'LLMs jump to solutions' generalizes from one self-evaluated preprint and one hackathon.
fix: In one 48-hour hackathon (Egea et al. 2024) a ChatGPT-4-led team placed second of six but abandoned promising concepts after minor difficulties, added needless complexity and showed design fixation; an unreviewed preprint (O'Hara) reports that LLM assistants tend to accept a user's technology choice without validating requirements and proposes a Five Whys workflow, whose reported detection rate and cost could not be checked.

R-Zero numbers verified (+5.51 math, pseudo-label accuracy 79.0 to 63.0 over three iterations, smallest 0.6B peaks at step 15 while the 4B model declines only at step 60), but in Young and Bjorner the ledger, follow-up half-life and re-checks are described as design choices whose removal effects are only predicted (Table 7), not shown to be needed.
fix: Co-evolving loops degrade without a bound: R-Zero gained +5.51 math points over three iterations while pseudo-label accuracy fell from 79.0 to 63.0 percent, and the smallest model peaked at step 15 (larger models declined later); the Microsoft theory-loop (Comet-H) design includes a grounding ledger, a half-life on carried follow-ups and re-checks of claims against code, but the paper only predicts, and does not test, what removing them would cause.

All Finance/PlanCraft/SWE-bench/aggregate/error-amplification numbers match Kim et al.-style scaling paper; Massoudi 6 nodes, about 650 s vs 38.6 s match; in the scaling paper the error-amplification main effect was not significant after controls (p=0.658) and D is a domain-complexity score (Finance 0.41 vs PlanCraft 0.42), the paper attributes the contrast to parallelizable vs sequential subtasks.

The three Hastie-Pennington chapter lines are one document and the 1992 experiments are the same authors' own tests, so the story-model description rests on a single lab; the independent OpenLearn summary (blocked) is a secondary account that itself lists critiques.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model proposes that jurors build a causal story from the evidence, learn verdict categories from the instructions, and match story to category, so the verdict rests on the story summary; the supporting experiments (Pennington and Hastie 1992, three mock-juror studies) come from the same research group and Bayesian or linear-updating models fit item-by-item judgments better.

problem: In the Hastie-Pennington chapter this is a theoretical implication of the model ('This means that... jurors will be swayed...'), not a measured result, and it is the authors' own advice to judges; the emotion mock-jury study (PMC12292101) tests affect-driven evidence evaluation, not under-weighting of credibility or inference-chain strength relative to an ideal evaluator, and the Czaban item is a Hungarian secondary relay.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model predicts that, compared with an ideal evidence evaluator, jurors will be swayed by the consistency and plausibility of a story and under-weight source credibility and inference-chain strength, and they advise judges to stress procedural instructions on credibility and inferential strength; this is a model-derived prediction, with no quantified effect in the sources opened.

problem: The five properties and the uniqueness rule are Hastie and Pennington's theoretical certainty principles (one chapter listed three times, plus their own 1996 article); the only independent check, Willmott et al. 2018, is a scale validation giving 'early evidence' of the certainty-principle process, not a demonstration that acceptance and confidence track each property.
fix: Hastie and Pennington's Story Model holds that acceptance and confidence depend on a story's coverage, completeness, consistency, plausibility and uniqueness, and that two coherent stories lower confidence; independent support is limited to a scale validation (Willmott et al. 2018, n=324) that reports early evidence for this certainty-principle process.

problem: Numbers check out (Silicon Crowd 0.17 to 0.14 and 0.22 to 0.15, AIA 0.096 vs 0.109, BLF 58.3 vs 62.7 and KNN 59.1 vs 50.0, Pratt weighted 0.2540 worst), but in Hsieh the 'ETH 8% by count' is the model's own arithmetic (50+20+10 days of 1003, written in its answer, not a code or data count), the BLF full agent beats the empirical-prior baseline significantly (+4.5 BI), so 'strong baseline' is not 'no better', and the Pratt pipeline lacks a data-anchored control.
fix: Giving LLMs a crowd or market value helped (GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14, Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 with the human median; market price alone 0.096 vs 0.109 for the best prior LLM system; ForecastBench top LLMs used freeze values), while model-recalled base rates are vague and gave no gain (Hsieh's trace recalls 30% for ETH, then reasons its way to 8% with day counts the model wrote itself; Pratt's recalled-base-rate pipeline had the worst weighted Brier, 0.2540). A code-computed class frequency was a strong baseline (empirical prior Brier Index 58.3 on dataset questions vs 62.7 for the full BLF agent, which still beats it significantly; KNN frequency counter 59.1 vs 50.0 for always-0.5).

problem: Buehler et al. numbers all match (37 contacted, analysis on 33: 33.9 vs 55.5, 29.7%, worst case 48.6; Study 4 N=123 recall-relevant removes mean bias but not absolute error; Study 5 observers 48.0% vs 2.4% mention past); Thomas and Koenig was opened in the primary PMC paper (not secondary as the claim says) and supports less bias when the first task was the same.

Martingale scores (0.037, 0.086, 0.103), the ~0.04 worse-than-chance remark and the BayesBench active-vs-passive pro-user bias all check out, but Table 1 of He et al. shows the system-prompt effects are not consistent across models in forecasting (critical-thinking prompt raised the score for GPT-4o and Maverick and lowered it for R1, Flash and Scout; prior-conforming raised it for most but not Gemini Flash), and the Martingale result concerns the model's own prior belief, not a user-stated stance.
fix: Across forecasting, value-laden and paper-review tasks, LLM belief updates were predictable from the model's own prior belief (Martingale scores with chain of thought 0.037 forecasting, 0.086 paper review, 0.103 ChangeMyView), and a score near 0.04 coincided with forecasts worse than chance; prompting to conform to the prior generally raised the score and a critical-thinking prompt lowered it only for some models. Separately, in BayesBench's social-judgment task, actively engaging with a simulated user produced a persistent pro-user bias that passive reading of the same evidence did not. Neither study tested removing the stance at the evidence-search step.

problem: GSM8K step-wise numbers, TextCraft depth 2 and 3 numbers and the kth-letter result all match, but the TextCraft numbers cited do not show a gain growing with depth: the absolute ADaPT gain shrinks from +51.3 points at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2) to +36.9 at depth 3 (1.8 to 38.7), and the comparison is against ReAct, not chain of thought.
fix: Decomposition helps more on longer problems in least-to-most (GSM8K 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07 for chain of thought) and in decomposed prompting (kth-letter concatenation stays near 100% while chain of thought falls with length), and was worse on 2-step GSM8K (74.53 vs 76.68); ADaPT still lifts TextCraft at depth 3 (ReAct 1.8 to 38.7) though its absolute gain is smaller than at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2).

problem: Hirtz et al. (no measured benefit; repeatability study cited), Gericke and Eisenbart ('initial empirical evidence') and the Clemson abstract ('little experimental evidence' for ideation) match, but 'only repeatability and usage-frequency studies exist' is wider than the sources: Gericke cites further empirical studies (Caldwell 2011, Srinivasan 2012, Sen 2013) and the same dissertation and the Linsey and Booth experiments in this note are ideation experiments.
fix: Evidence that function modelling helps designers is thin: the functional-basis authors report no measurement of benefit beyond a repeatability study, a 2017 review calls the empirical evidence for its benefits 'initial' (citing Kurfman, Caldwell, Srinivasan and Sen studies), and a Clemson dissertation abstract says there is little experimental evidence that function models help concept generation (the few experiments on it show no reliable gain).

problem: BCC 0.477-0.743, gradients 0.295-0.482, direction agreement 63.7-75.8% (Imran et al. Table 1); Filbry et al. cross-chat Dutch-book violations above 50% of 30 scenarios, within-dialogue 10% (Gemini) or 1 of 30 (Gemma), reasoning and code results match; Wu 2026 not needed; the abstract page alone did not show these numbers, full text did.

Simon's Hora and Tempus (about 4,000 times, 1/111 x 20 x 20,000) and ten-dial safe (100^10, about 10 x 50 = 500 tries with clicks) match the original; Ulrich (1995) defines modular vs integral architecture and does not corroborate the numbers, so the quantitative claim rests on Simon alone (an analytic parable, as the claim says).

Plan-and-Solve numbers are mislabeled: in the PS paper's table 56.4/57.0/59.3 on GSM8K are Zero-shot-CoT/PoT/PS+; plain PS is 58.2 on GSM8K (+1.8 over CoT, not +0.6) and its six-dataset average is 72.9 (not 73.5, which is PoT). Least-to-most +1.5, self-planning pass@10 76.3 vs 75.0 and pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1, and the Meincke GPQA results (o4-mini +0.056 at one threshold, 20 to 80% more time) match; PS models were text-davinci-003, not strong models.
fix: Plan-first prompting gives small gains over plain chain of thought (about 1 to 7 points; plain Plan-and-Solve +1.8 on GSM8K, 56.4 to 58.2, and PS+ +2.9; least-to-most +1.5 on GSM8K), mainly by cutting missing-step errors. Self-planning gains shrink with sampling: pass@10 is 76.3 vs 75.0 direct, against pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1. For reasoning models generic step-by-step prompting added almost nothing on GPQA Diamond (only o4-mini +5.6 points at one threshold) and cost 20 to 80% more time.

problem: Press et al. (about 40% gap; 42.9% ChatGPT, 23.0% GPT-4) and Dziri et al. (3x3 multiplication ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%) match; Press itself warns the GPT-4 figure may be invalid because the dataset predates GPT-4 and could be in its training data.

Table 8.1 of the Pennington-Hastie chapter (N=130; 59, 78, 31, 63) and the 1992 replication (N=414, equal total recall, different clustering) match; Czaban's relay reports 62% instead of 63% for both-witness; the replication and original are the same research group, and the chapter gives no verdict percentages for the 1992 study.

Booth 2013 (26 students, n=78 trees, no method effect) and Booth 2015 study 2 (n=78, r=0.075, p=0.515) match, but Booth 2013 compares three decomposition methods with each other and measures functions, errors and abstraction levels, not idea count or design quality against a no-decomposition control; Booth 2015 study 2 is observational; the Linsey 2005 figures (n=54, 19.0 vs 19.7) could not be opened (ASEE page blocked; only an abstract saying function modelling was indistinguishable from control was reachable) and the quoted evidence line itself lists group sizes of 5 and 7.
fix: In human studies, evidence that a functional decomposition step improves ideas or design quality is absent: a first controlled test (Linsey et al. 2005) reported no difference from a control group, a within-subject comparison of three decomposition methods (Booth 2013, 26 students) found no method effect on its measures, and an observational study of 78 industry reports (Booth 2015 study 2) found no correlation between using decomposition and design grade (r=0.075, p=0.515). All tests are small, observational or preliminary, so a small benefit is not excluded.

problem: Phalen et al. 2025 (N=713, 677, 651) confirmed but the authors call it correlational/mediational, and the second source (Thagard, scanned PDF) was unreadable and is about OJ polls, not re-weighting by a leading verdict.
fix: In three mock-jury studies (N=713, 677, 651), greater negative emotion toward the defendant was associated, via mediation, with more agreement with unrelated plaintiff evidence and less with unrelated defence evidence, and with more liable verdicts; judicial rehabilitation did not reduce this (correlational, single lab).

problem: Bessis et al. (single paper, listed several times) numbers all verified; human recency in Bessis and law-student study (Maegherman et al., N=407) also verified.
Numbers (2,304; 63.56 vs 58.82; 21% vs 49%) verified in Sun et al., but only some effects replicated: reporting delay did not (LLMs sensitive, humans not); Wu 2026 does not test level divergence.
fix: LLM mock jurors diverge from humans in level (guilt probability 63.56 vs 58.82 but guilty verdicts 21% vs 49%; 2,304 responses); the defendant-race bias and the rise with more allegations replicated, but sensitivity to reporting delay appeared only in the LLMs.

problem: Dalal et al. (ACL 2024 / arXiv versions are one paper) verified: consistency similar for correct/incorrect, depth +6% and drift +10%, up to 77% vs 50% random; abstract wording is '+17%' vs table avg +17.5%; claim's 'up to 77%' holds. Douven source is a different topic.

Test of Time Table 7 numbers match, but for GPT-4 shuffle (60.71) is not the lowest (StartTimeAndRelation 60.54); the paper's 'consistently lowest' is slightly off, 'at equal tokens' is not stated; premise-order drops are up to 20-30 points for GPT-4-turbo/PaLM 2-L (about 16-21 at 12 rules) and over 40 only for weaker models, not a uniform 20 to 40+.
fix: Reordering the same facts changes LLM accuracy: on Test of Time shuffled facts score at or near the lowest (GPT-4 60.71 vs 65.36 best; Gemini 1.5 Pro 63.04 vs 75.00; Claude-3-Sonnet 45.71 vs 73.57), and in deduction (Chen et al. 2024) forward (proof-order) premises beat other orders for every model, by up to 20-30 points for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L and by over 40 points for weaker models such as Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo.

problem: Kriegsspiel page (Prussia only army wargaming, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Zenko (19 ships, $250M, 752-page report, end state scripted) and IFPV (+19.4% relative gain in a different setup than Table 3) verified; 'unequal compute' is an inference since the paper reports no compute figures; negative 'no controlled test found' not checkable.

Kriegsspiel page (Reisswitz umpire, dice, 1:8000 maps, Meckel/Verdy du Vernois), Snow Globe (control adjudicates, adjudication hardest, 'Include unexpected consequences' with Mistral-7B-OpenOrca) and WarAgent (secretary agent verifies actions, up to 4 exchanges) verified; Kriegsspiel two listings are one Wikipedia page.

Payne (21 games, 29-64%) and Adl & Williams (3,604 games, 10.7% to 28.6%) verified, but Solopova et al. does not show models pick more cooperative actions than graduate students (only their explanations are cooperative in framing; some models were more coercive on economic choices), and Payne's models did sometimes reduce violence (return to start line) though never chose accommodation or withdrawal.
fix: In Payne's 21 model-vs-model nuclear-crisis games no model ever chose accommodation or surrender (only de-escalation as far as returning to the start line) and strategic-threat level was reached in 29-64% of games depending on the model; in Solopova et al.'s menu simulations models' explanations were cooperative in framing but their actions were mixed against graduate-student players (some more coercive); one-line framing moved escalation from 10.7% to 28.6% in 3,604 games (Adl and Williams). No Lamparth replication with experts was found.

Zeng and Zhang: error up 46.20 / down 30.28 / unchanged 23.52 percent, anti-anchoring cut prior-directed shift but not error (it raised error; tested on Qwen3-8B only), evidence-validation rule traded coverage for reliability; DERELAB only corroborates anchoring generally (anchoring rates 0.43-0.48 for GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-32B).

Laban et al. (FlipFlop): ten LLMs, seven tasks, flip 46 percent of the time, average accuracy drop 17 percent, verified; BeliefScope corroborates that pressure and evidence both move outputs. The closing sentence is a prescriptive conclusion.

DERELAB (GPT-5-mini C2-eff 95.4 vs C2 acc 20.3) and STALE (Qwen3.5-27B Type I SR 76.0 vs IPA 39.0) verified; 'premise resistance mostly under 5 percent' holds for most systems but not all (Gemini-3.1-pro reaches 30.0 on Type I PR).

DeltaLogic numbers match (Qwen3-1.7B 0.667/0.467/0.600 n=30; Qwen3-4B 0.650/0.450/0.600 n=20; Phi-4-mini 0.950/0.850; the four DeltaLogic entries are one paper); DERELAB (anchoring), STALE (outdated-memory failures) and BeliefShift (models miss legitimate updates) corroborate; ClawArena not opened.

Minor: circumscription gives a disjunction rather than multiple extensions, and Reiter default logic itself has no specificity priority (SEP); claim's 'families agree' is slightly broad but supported by SEP/McCarthy.
Figures are easy-split intrusion rates (GPT-5.1 hard 1.2, Qwen3-32B thinking hard 2.6); DeltaLogic n is only 20-30 episodes per model.

Minor: FlipFlop reports '17%' average accuracy drop (taken as points); Simpson et al. note an April replication drifted (89.7 to 98.5 percent), and the 7-to-4 / 20 false positive result is from a single model and 68 scenarios.
The 'about 60 main schemes' figure is not in the three listed sources (SEP gives 96); it comes from Visser et al. 2021 in another claim. Pinto/Kock caveat that CQs often cannot shift burden.

Minor: tuning claim is a one-sentence remark (results not shown, and the paper elsewhere says no prompt tuning was done); the 67.6 is a manual evaluation of the best submission whose automatic score was 50.0; shared-task overview shares authors with the benchmark paper.

Both numbers match, but the 39.44 percent post-edits were mostly grammatical fixes (verb forms, plurals, double negations), not content repairs; the 68.28 to 72.22 result is one validation ablation where about 75 percent of labels were LLM-made.

LLM F1 0.65 is the best on the 7-scheme EthiX set only (Claude 3.5 few-shot reaches 0.72 on the 4-scheme EthiX4); and on QT30 1.0 is plain RoBERTa while 44.8 is the best of four training variants, so '1.0 to 44.8' is a range across configurations, not a drop.
fix: Scheme classification: trained annotators agree substantially (kappa 0.723 on a 10.2 percent sample for Walton schemes, 0.61 for the full guideline set); the best LLM reaches F1 0.65 on 686 real Kialo arguments over 7 schemes (0.72 on a 4-scheme subset); the same LLMs score 0.98-0.99 on machine-written textbook arguments; and a scheme classifier that scores 99.2 F1 on textbook text gets only 1.0 on real QT30 dialogue, rising to 44.8 with scheme families and dialogue training. Cause to effect and expert opinion are the most misclassified schemes.

problem: Minor: 'does not transfer' is slightly loose, since plain RoBERTa gets 1.0 F1 on QT30 and the best variant (scheme families plus dialogue data) reaches 44.8; 89.1 percent is NLAS-CQ (GPT-generated) while EN 74.8 percent is NLAS-multi, and NLAS-multi Spanish kappa was only 0.22.
Numbers match; GPT-judged MT-Bench with 5 models and ArgMed with 300 items per set; the 'no token-matched best-of-N comparison' part is an absence claim that cannot be checked from these papers.
Minor: Stechly Blocksworld shows LLM critique helping (40 to 55), so 'does not help' holds on most but not all domains; 8-87 is the sound first-error-feedback column.

Huang et al. say debate with 3 responses is slightly BETTER than self-consistency at 3 responses (SC 82.5); debate only falls below SC at equal counts of 6 and 9 (debate 83.2 and 83.0 vs SC 85.3 and 88.2).
fix: At equal calls or tokens, majority voting over samples matches or beats model-run critique and debate, except at large budgets: on GSM8K (GPT-3.5) self-consistency scores 82.5, 85.3 and 88.2 at 3, 6 and 9 responses, debate is only slightly better at 3 responses and clearly below at 6 and 9 (83.2, 83.0); a fine-tuned generative verifier needed about 8x compute to match self-consistency and 128x to gain 3.8 points on MATH; sampling with a sound verifier and no critique text kept most of the gain of critique with a sound verifier.

problem: Actual-persuasiveness half rests on one 2001 experiment (324 readers, one claim about a cultural centre) from the Nijmegen group that also supplied the comparison data for Hornikx 2008; Hornikx concludes expectations are 'generally accurate', so 'only partly match' leans on Hoeken alone.
fix: In one experiment (324 readers, one claim), statistical evidence persuaded more than anecdotal or causal evidence, which were equally unconvincing; lay people rank expected persuasiveness statistical > expert > causal > anecdotal and in a comparison with an earlier study from the same group these expectations were generally accurate, although in the 2001 experiment perceived (causal over anecdotal) and actual persuasiveness did not correspond.

problem: Minor: Lou and Sun test mostly GPT-4/GPT-4o (GPT-3.5 varied), and SynAnchors reports one method (Anti-DP) that lowers Llama anchoring 34.7 to 24.7, so 'fail' means simple prompt strategies.

SACD's own tables show self-help rewriting is no better than (finance 0.1885 vs vanilla 0.1648) or worse than (legal 0.4590 vs 0.3840) plain prompting, and weaker on small models; only GPT-4 BiasBuster and the iterated SACD loop reliably cut bias.
fix: Rewriting the biasing text with a model-run loop cuts measured bias when the cue is planted in the text: the iterated SACD loop beat vanilla, CoT and self-help in every domain by its third round, and one-pass self-help worked on GPT-4 (framing gap -0.405 to -0.010) and gpt-4o but was no better than or worse than vanilla prompting in the finance and legal domains and on small models.

problem: Minor: Huang et al. is the direct evidence (oracle GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7); the other listed sources are anchoring studies where reflection or self-improving prompts did not help, which is looser support for 'accuracy'.

Minor: Wang et al. report 9.8% and 14.3% accuracy gain in human alignment (not necessarily points); math grading figures are 14/20 to 3/20 on 10 questions with swapped positions; the 2026 gap numbers match Kumar et al. Table 2.

BiasBuster says few-shot 'can lead to failure cases' for some biases and models (Llama-2-7b contrastive admit rates 0.996/1.000), not 'often'; Itzhak et al. only find that same-task examples reduce bias less than format-only examples (they do not show the examples carry the bias), and format few-shot slightly lowered bias in most models.
fix: Few-shot debiasing exemplars can break some models (Llama-2-7b answers collapsing to nearly all-admit or all-reject on several BiasBuster setups), gave no gain for GPT-4 framing, and scored poorly against other methods in SACD; examples taken from the same task reduced bias less than format-only examples in Itzhak et al.

problem: Hagendorff et al.'s 96 percent (GPT-4) is on 50 bespoke, newly written CRT-style tasks per type, not just the famous items, and training exposure is the authors' speculation; the evidence that perturbed items still expose errors is only Binz and Schulz on GPT-3 (adversarial vignettes), not frontier models. The three Hagendorff entries are one paper.
fix: On newly written CRT-style tasks ChatGPT-4 answers 96 percent correctly (ChatGPT-3.5 59, GPT-3 davinci-003 5), which the authors tentatively attribute to training on CRT-like tasks; in older GPT-3, the original CRT items were all answered intuitively wrong and adversarially altered vignettes produced non-human errors (Binz and Schulz), but no source shows perturbed items still trapping frontier models.

problem: Sources show presence of biases, not human-like size: ChatGPT anchoring gap was 85 (20.83 vs 105.97) versus 58 for humans (22.5 vs 80.5), SynAnchors say most LLMs are the same as or worse than humans, and Malberg et al. find some effects (status quo, disposition) opposite to humans; Jones and Steinhardt show accuracy loss from anchoring lines in code, not a human-comparable size.
fix: LLMs show anchoring, framing, availability and related effects on many tasks, including code generation, but the size differs from humans (e.g. GPT-3.5 anchoring gap about 85 vs 58 for humans in one small study) and some biases such as status quo and disposition effect run opposite to the human direction.

problem: Croskerry et al. say awareness 'does not guarantee' debiasing and the field has been gloomy, and list feedback and educational tools, but neither paper tests telling people to be fair or unbiased, nor shows practice with feedback and task redesign 'work better'; Sellier et al. is a primary study (one-shot game training, 29 percent fewer confirming choices), not a secondary source.
fix: Secondary reviews say that raising awareness of bias does not by itself guarantee debiasing, while training with feedback (for example game-based training, which in one field study cut a confirmation-biased choice by 29 percent) and supportive environments are proposed as stronger routes; no source tested 'be fair or unbiased' instructions directly.

problem: The review does not find 'little evidence' of effect: it finds few studies (12 of 52 screened tested retention of at least 14 days, 1 tested far transfer) and most of those reported retained benefit, especially for games over videos; Sellier et al. report transfer (29 percent fewer confirming choices). Willingham is off-topic for debiasing training.
fix: A systematic review of debiasing studies found only 12 of 52 screened studies that tested retention (14 days or more) and just 1 that tested far transfer; most retention studies showed lasting benefit, mainly for game-based training, and the single transfer study (Sellier et al. 2019) found trained participants 29 percent less likely to make the confirmation-biased choice, so evidence is thin rather than negative.

problem: Both usable sources are by Willingham (2007 and 2016) and the 2016 brief repeats the 2007 argument; the third listed source (Sellier et al.) does not address critical-thinking programmes; no effect sizes are given for 'mostly ineffective'.
fix: Willingham (2007, 2016) argues, without citing effect sizes, that critical thinking is not a general skill that transfers across domains, that domain knowledge and practice decide performance, and that the programmes sold after 1983 were not very effective.

problem: Minor: figures are from the Kumar et al. audit (6 judges, 4 datasets); the 7-17 percent replication figure is the paper's range across cells.

Minor: Langley 1977 notes BACON uses a programmer-specified artificial world and cannot handle noise; the 'sufficiency not history' caveat is the claim's own interpretation, not stated in those papers.

Minor: 'recalled, not discovered' is the authors' inference (they write 'suggest'); LLM-SR and LLM-SRBench are the same lab; SR-Scientist's 'nearly 50 percent reached sufficiently small error' is not the same as solved, and it sits in tension with LLM-SRBench calling LSR-Transform hard.

Minor: the 2.1-7.2 vs 10.8-31.5 symbolic accuracy figures all come from one paper (LLM-SRBench, Table 1); LLM-SR also differs from direct prompting by more than the loop (program skeleton, buffer), so it is not a clean loop-only ablation.
Minor: ablation is one problem (Oscillation 2) with one backbone (GPT-3.5); Ma et al. imaginary-law test confirmed in Table 4; both sources are different labs.

The 'about 54% pooled correct' is Yang & Johnson-Laird Exp 1 correct rate over ALL quantified illusions (possibility 23%, impossibility 67%), not illusions of impossibility alone; other numbers (15/91 N=20, 19/95, 6/83 N=80 r=.87) check out.
fix: Illusory inferences are systematic: confident, uniform errors on problems where reasoning from true cases only gives a wrong answer. Found with propositional, embedded-disjunction, quantified, modal and conditional problems. Human rates from originals: modal 15% correct vs 91% on controls (N=20), embedded disjunctions 19% vs 95%, conditionals 6% vs 83% (N=80, Spanish lab, r=.87, only partly independent of the Johnson-Laird network). Illusions of impossibility are weaker than illusions of possibility (quantified problems, Yang & Johnson-Laird: 67% vs 23% correct; 54% pooled over both kinds). LLMs also produce the predicted fallacies on disjunction problems (d01, d02), though those tests are by a rival theory's authors and have no matched controls. Gap pass: an independent lab (Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas 2021, N=64 and 70 analysed) found the disjunction illusion again with controls at 87%/26% and 90%/20% accepted, and showed it is triggered by knowledge links, not only word overlap (d24).

problem: Cited confidence values match Goldvarg and Johnson-Laird, Espino et al. and Khemlani and Johnson-Laird; JL&S 1999 not opened; note Yang and Johnson-Laird found a small reliable confidence gap (.13), and 4 of 5 sources are one lab.

Numbers match (80/21, 92/51, 98/72/8), but every source is a Johnson-Laird-lab paper (Bucciarelli, Khemlani, Goodwin, all co-authored by the theory's author); no outside lab replicates the model-count effect, and the relational 98/72/8 is cited from earlier work.

In Bucciarelli and Johnson-Laird, no-valid-conclusion items (50%, 41% in Exp 2) are harder than one-model items (80%) but easier than multiple-model items (21%), so it is not 'the hard case' for humans; the LLM part (rarely say 'nothing follows', ICL does not fix it) is supported by Eisape et al. and Bertolazzi et al.
fix: 'Nothing follows' is a hard case for humans and a very hard one for LLMs. Humans do worse on no-valid-conclusion items (50% in Exp 1) than on one-model items (80%), though better than on multiple-model items (21%) (Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird); LLMs rarely produce it (PaLM 2, Pythia, LLaMA) and drift to form-based (atmosphere) answers; in-context examples did not fix it for the open models.

problem: Numbers verified (5.6 vs 1.1 unbiased, 56% violations N=39, 53% vs 8% cited second-hand from Girotto and Gonzalez), but both papers are Johnson-Laird-lab work testing his own theory; the Bayesian rescue figure is only a citation; the notes' 'r=.76' is actually R2.

51/21 and 74/92 match Johnson-Laird 2010 (a self-review of one cited study); but the 228 experiments show people select instances, counterexamples or both (not simply 'default confirming'), and the feedback switch comes from the repeated selection task, not the 228-study meta-analysis; both sources are model-theory authors' work.
fix: In Wason selection tasks people select instances of the hypothesis, its potential counterexamples, or both, depending on content and instructions (meta-analysis of 228 experiments, Ragni & Kola 2018); with feedback in the repeated selection task they switched from instances to potential counterexamples. When judging given conclusions, counterexample use was higher and correct rejection lower for conclusions merely consistent with the premises than for inconsistent ones (use 51% vs 21%; correct rejection 74% vs 92%; Johnson-Laird 2010, citing one study).

problem: Mondorf and Plank (31.7% Llama-2-70B sound, symbolic strategy only occasional) and Eisape et al. (NVC accuracy near 0%) match; note Zephyr-7B uses the symbolic strategy most often among tested models, and the closing design inference is the notes' own.

Chen et al. say permuting premise order 'can cause' a drop of over 30% (a maximum, not a drop shown for each listed model); the 14%, 7% and +4% figures (11 LLMs), and the 13-22% moral-judgment order effects match their abstracts.
fix: Premise order and counterfactual content hurt LLM deduction. Permuting premise order can cause accuracy drops of over 30% (Chen et al. 2024; models tested include GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). Premises that contradict world knowledge cost an average 14% across 11 models; a flag-and-reason prompt cut the gap to 7% and raised overall accuracy 4%. Note the Johnson-Laird view predicts order effects (model construction is serial) and belief effects (believable conclusions stop search), but neither paper tests it. Gap pass: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models for deduction was found; d26 is training-based on 7B-70B models and d27 shows order effects of 13-22% in frontier models on moral judgments only.

problem: Numbers match (Dong et al. 47.27->56.64, 77.39->80.01, 111 and 51 tasks; Jha et al. 19/20 vs 2/20), but Dong's feedback was only 'your answer is not correct' (no counterexample), and the Jha figures are GPT-4 baseline success by problem size, not a measured effect of counterexample feedback, so 'counterexample feedback helps but is weak' is not shown.
fix: An external checker telling ChatGPT that its answer is wrong (no counterexample content) improved it only slowly: gpt-3.5 rose from 47.27% to 56.64% and gpt-4o from 77.39% to 80.01% on 256 syllogism satisfiability tasks over up to 10 rounds, with 111 and 51 tasks never solved (Dong et al.). Separately, in blocks-world planning GPT-4 alone solved 19/20 problems at 3 blocks and 2/20 at 10 blocks, and Jha et al. use solver counterexamples in an LLM loop, but that paper's baseline numbers here do not measure how much counterexample feedback helps.

problem: Oaksford and Chater 1994 and Sperber et al. 1995 (independent labs) support the 4% and ~10% logical rates; the 46%/33% modal figures come from Johnson-Laird and Wason (1970), quoted second-hand, while the 34-task pooled counts support the general pattern.

Klayman and Ha (positive test strategy as general default heuristic; fails when H lies inside T) and Wason 1960 (29 subjects, 6 correct first time) match; the conditions for soundness rest on the single Klayman and Ha paper.
Jhaveri et al. (6% to 78%, eleven LLMs, I:C correlates with success) and Bertolazzi et al. (12 LLMs, Spearman -0.779, p=0.003) match; two independent groups.

Numbers match, but the general claim is too strong: in FalsifyBench the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned models; Jhaveri's Gemini-2.5-Pro vs small non-thinking comparison confounds scale (thinking helped Qwen3 but without a consistent rise in disconfirming tests); and on WILT the best model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 14/50) is not a reasoning model, with o1-mini 13 and o1-preview 12.
fix: Larger reasoning (thinking) models generally do better at rule discovery and falsify more: GPT-5.2-Chat 75 percent and GPT-OSS-120B 68 percent vs 33 to 41 percent for instruction-tuned models (FalsifyBench), although the smallest reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse than all instruction-tuned ones; Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) 0.73 vs 0.06 to 0.33 for small non-thinking models (Jhaveri, confounded with scale). On WILT no model solves more than 14 of 50 and the best (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is not a reasoning model.

problem: Dasgupta et al. (z>2.2 for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5, humans; marginal 1.78) and Seals and Shalin (chance 1/6, mostly 0.06-0.29) match, but Seals and Shalin found that social content does benefit LLMs (significant social-rule by content interaction; realistic social > realistic non-social), only less than in humans (about 30% vs about 70%), so 'weak or absent' overstates.
fix: LLMs show the human content effect on the Wason task: realistic rules beat arbitrary ones (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans, all z>2.2; only marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2). Small open models mostly fail the standard form (0.06 to 0.29, chance 1/6). In one study the social-rule advantage in LLMs was real but much smaller than in humans (about 30% vs about 70% solved).

problem: Numbers check (Maegherman n=27: 22.2% correct, 40.7% confirming only; maths majors and mathematicians under 50% in Dasgupta et al.; Swann and Giuliano F(1,47)=4.161), but the judges' task was a leaves-and-pot variation, not the abstract task, with n=27 and the thesis itself calls 22% a relatively good result against the typical under 10%.
fix: Confirmatory choices remain common in trained people: in a small survey (n=27) of Dutch judges on a Wason variant, 40.7% chose only the confirming option and 22.2% gave the correct confirming-plus-falsifying pair (the thesis reads this as relatively good versus the typical under 10%); undergraduate maths majors and academic mathematicians scored under 50% on the arbitrary abstract task (Dasgupta et al., citing others); and in social interviews people favour confirmatory questions, especially when certain (Swann and Giuliano).

problem: Parab et al. (4.3% of semantically wrong hypotheses yielded a program passing the training examples, 5,500 trials GPT-4o) and Moghe and Chin (N=1 never above 45.5%, N=5 57.5% pass@2, refinement only -0.75pp) match; Chari and Pattanaik's EIG result is about a support mismatch with the generator, so the EIG sentence is the notes' inference, and Parab also finds the summarizer step loses about a quarter of correct hypotheses.

Cosmides et al. 2010 ('only 5-30%' on indicative rules, 65-80% on social contracts) and Klauer et al. 2007 ('typically fewer than 10%' P and not-Q) support it; the 5-30% range is Cosmides' summary, not a pooled meta-analysis, and Fiddick and Cosmides sources share a lab.

Fiddick 2003 (realistic rules failed to replicate Wason and Shapiro; Manktelow and Evans 1979), Cosmides et al. 2010 and Kroger et al. 1993 (permission 47% vs arbitrary 5% only with violation-checking plus explicit negatives) support it; Fiddick and Cosmides are the same theoretical camp, while Kroger/Cheng/Holyoak and Sperber/Girotto are independent rivals.

Cosmides 2010 (64/46/26 additive factors, 5-30% indicative), Cosmides 1989 pages via 2010 summary, and Gigerenzer and Hug (n=93, 94% vs 44%) match; minor slip: Cosmides' familiar descriptive control was 46%/38%, just above the stated 45% top of the control range; the claim already flags that 65-80 is one lab's spread.

Sperber and Girotto 2002 Exp 2 (N=120, 33%/43% vs 10%/0% P and not-Q) and Gigerenzer and Hug 1992 (perspective flips P and not-Q 75% to not-P and Q 61%) match; independent labs; note Sperber and Girotto's cheater cells were below Fiddick et al.'s original (33% vs 66% failed replication).

Lampinen et al. (Wason z>2.2, NLI no effect with ceiling, item-level t(832)=3.49, t(345)=4.98) and Ando et al. NeuBAROCO (GPT-3.5 31.37% inconsistent vs 61.05% symbolic) match; the NLI null is partly due to ceiling effects, and the claim omits that stronger models show little belief effect (see K12).

Lampinen et al. (Chinchilla 5-shot Wason content effects exaggerated), Bertolazzi et al. 2025 (CE 0.348 to 0.096; 0.213 to 0.014 with CoT) and Bertolazzi et al. 2024 (LLaMA-3 8B 70.74 to 52.59, LLaMA-2-inst 7B 32.22 to 19.26) match; 'ICL often cut accuracy' rests on other sources I did not open.

Cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, debias vector CE 0.348 to 0.072, and K-CAST up to 15% absolute match, but 'not reachable by a text scaffold' is contradicted by the same Bertolazzi et al. paper, where chain-of-thought alone cut CE 0.348 to 0.096 and 0.213 to 0.014; also the two Bertolazzi entries are versions of one paper.
fix: Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded and aligned inside open models (cosine 0.48 to 0.64 vs 0.10 to 0.17 for controls); a debias vector cut CE from 0.348 to 0.072 and conditional activation steering (K-CAST) gave up to 15 points absolute on models that static steering could not fix. Chain-of-thought prompting alone also cut CE substantially in strong open models (0.348 to 0.096), so text prompting reaches part of the effect, while steering offers a further internal lever.

problem: GSM-Symbolic found accuracy falls when numbers (or names plus numbers) change, but changing names alone leaves GSM8K performance near the name-changed distribution (only extra variance); the 65% figure is a maximum and Wu et al. report 'substantial and consistent' degradation over 11 tasks (not verified per task).
fix: Models are brittle to surface content beyond logic tasks: changing numerical values lowers GSM accuracy (changing names alone mainly adds variance), adding one irrelevant but plausible clause drops accuracy by up to 65 percent (GSM-NoOp), and on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks performance degrades substantially and consistently relative to the default versions (Wu et al.).

problem: Ahn and Graham (n=22; control P and not-Q .18), Macchi et al. (control 4%/10%; Necessarily 66%/77%) and Kroger et al. (47% vs 5%) match; minor slip: n=130 is Macchi's Exp 1 control sample, the 'necessarily' groups are smaller (N=82 combined), and Ahn and Graham's 50% is a mean over three explicated conditions rather than the same measure as the control's 18% P and not-Q.

FOLIO 93.8 vs 74.1 (81 items), Symbolic Tree ChatGPT 71.8 vs 53.7, and Phi-3-mini over 65% NoOp drop all match; slip: the 65% drop is for the irrelevant clause (NoOp), not for name or number swaps, and name-only swaps do not clearly lower accuracy.

Eisape et al. (about 75% vs about 50%, near 0% on 'nothing follows', 30 samples at temp 0.5, binary discrimination markedly higher on those items) and Bertolazzi et al. (pretrained LLaMA/Pythia rarely say 'nothing follows') match; the 'does this conclusion follow' wording is the notes' description of Eisape's binary-validity method.

Wu et al. (93.8 vs 74.1 on 81 FOLIO items; consistent drops on 11 tasks), Tang et al. (70.1 vs 71.8), and Saparov and He (true ontology allows skipping hops) match; Kim et al. only report 'evidence of partial contamination' from extra attention heads, so 'inject world knowledge' is stated more firmly than the paper; 'so it was using memory' is Tang's inference.

Ozeki et al. (87/90 = 96.67%, 77.78 to 83.33; GPT-3.5 58.89 to 52.22/54.44), FregeLogic (Z3 74.7%, invalid 97.6, valid 52.2), LINC (syntax errors 38/24/13%) and Kartac et al. (95.83 vs 84.17, +11.7) all match; the closing 'weak link depends on size and data' is the notes' synthesis, and the Z3 figure comes from one SemEval system paper.

Kim et al. (recovery fails on belief-inconsistent data, 'suggesting' extra heads), Bertolazzi et al. (cosine 0.48-0.64 vs 0.10-0.17, alignment tracks content effect) and Valentino et al. (up to 15% absolute with K-CAST) match; hedged wording in Kim is firmer in the claim, Kim and Valentino share authors (Valentino, Freitas), and the claim is a three-paper synthesis with each finding resting on one paper.

Minor: the Maverick 3.83 to 10.11 and simple-CoT 5.24 figures come from the Phase 1 prompt comparison on a 200-sample inner subset (5.24 averaged over 3 models), not from the final SemEval ensemble; Tang numbers are only a pattern.
Lampinen Appx B.2 says PaLM 2-L scored over 75% in every Wason condition WITHOUT the prior correction (raw likelihood), not with prior-corrected scoring as the claim says; the other parts check out.
fix: Scoring method, answer format and run-to-run noise can swamp the content effect in measurements, so absolute numbers in this field are fragile. Lampinen: raw-likelihood scoring with an instruction prompt made several models answer 'valid' to everything on syllogisms, and on Wason, scoring without the prior correction gave PaLM 2-L over 75 percent in every condition (including arbitrary and nonsense) although Chinchilla got worse. Eisape: generative vs binary format changed 'nothing follows' accuracy from near 0 to 'markedly higher'. Macmillan-Scott: ten runs per prompt gave highly inconsistent answers. Poddar used adaptive majority voting. The direction of the content effect is broadly stable across scoring choices; the size is not.

problem: Stupple and Ball cells verified, but the aggregate 80% vs 33% comes only from a Wikipedia summary and is contradicted by the primary paper: Evans, Barston and Pollard (1983) Exp 1 shows believable 92% (valid) and 92% (invalid) vs unbelievable 46% and 8% (mean 92 vs 27), Exp 2 86/62/66/13, Exp 3 91/53/67/6.
fix: Believable conclusions are accepted far more often than unbelievable ones, and the pull is strongest on invalid arguments (accepting believable-invalid is the dominant error). Evans et al. (1983) Exp 1 (N=24) had valid-believable 92%, valid-unbelievable 46%, invalid-believable 92%, invalid-unbelievable 8% accepted; Stupple and Ball (2008, N=48) accepted 71% vs 36% of invalid believable vs unbelievable conclusions (figure AB-BC) and 61% vs 25% (figure BA-CB).

problem: Trippas 2014 (title is actually 'Fluency and belief bias in deductive reasoning: new indices for old effects', effect sizes are omega2), Markovits 2017 and Pennycook 2013 numbers verified; the analytic-disposition link is only indirect and the older-adults point rests on a secondary thesis with no numbers.

Claim rests on one paper (Lampinen et al., listed several times); its numbers check out, but high sensitivity/low specificity applies only to GPT-3.5 and larger PaLM 2, and Chinchilla and PaLM 2-M showed no significant validity x believability interaction. fix: In Knoblich et al. (1999) Exp 3 (N=34), tautological Type C was solved by 100% in Block 1 versus 61% for regular Type C (p<.001), and prior exposure to the tautological form shortened regular Type C solution times (p<.001) while Type D initial rate was unaffected (61% vs 69%, p=.64); Type D times also improved after exposure (p<.01), so the separation of constraint relaxation from chunk decomposition is supported for initial rates and only partly for times; this rests on one experiment from one lab.

problem: Minor: the 2001 eye-tracking study labels differ (its Problem C is a tight-chunk problem, so it does not test tautology), and the Knoblich lab papers (1999, 2001, Oellinger 2006) count as one lab; only Spiridonov 2025 is independent, so 'several labs' is really two.

Li et al. (2024) recalibrate each slice from k unlabeled examples (labelled data is needed only once, to train the recalibrator), so 'need labelled runs from the target slice' is not what the source shows; the k=5 to 20 result is target-precision success (0.81 at k=5), not an ECE gain.
fix: Calibration maps should be per task type, not global. Per-slice few-shot recalibration beat global temperature scaling in every setting tested (MMLU ECE 0.063 to 0.053 at PaLM2-L; 0.109 to 0.074 at LLaMA-65B) using only k=5 to 20 unlabeled examples from the target slice, although the recalibrator is trained once on labelled data from many slices; an agent calibrator learned on one domain transferred only partly (about 500 labelled trajectories per dataset). How many held-out items a counting-table map needs without training is not measured.

problem: Minor: the 54.8 to 92.7 GSM8K AUROC figures are GPT-3.5 (Table 3: CoT M=1 vs Self-Random M=5 with consistency), not GPT-4; claim does not name a model there.

fix: Raw verbalized confidence from open reasoning models is not good enough to drive control without recalibration: mean ECE 0.268 and AUROC 0.635 over 36 model-dataset pairs, against Cao's bar of ECE at most 0.15 and AUROC at least 0.60. Cao's Sonnet 4.6 numbers (JOL AUROC 0.745, FOK 0.612) are model-specific, and ECE and AUROC must be checked separately: Gemma 4 passes the joint ECE row (0.044) while its FOK AUROC fails (0.534) and its FOK ECE is 0.466.

problem: AgentAbstain reports post-hoc abstention (acting irreversibly and then claiming to abstain) in only 2.6% of abstain runs (about 10% for GPT-5.1/5.2), so 'often' is too strong; also the 53% to 91% threshold span is the GPT-5 pair only (other models exceed 91%, up to over 100%).
fix: When errors have explicit costs, models do not hold a stable act-or-escalate stance: implicit escalation thresholds differ widely, for example 53% (GPT-5-mini) to 91% (GPT-5-nano) accuracy within the GPT-5 family, and are not predicted by scale; in an agent benchmark abstention is largely independent of solving ability (best of 17 models 59.5% paired accuracy), and a minority of failures (post-hoc abstention, 2.6% of abstain runs overall, about 10% for GPT-5.1) come after an irreversible step. This supports a code-level cost threshold placed before irreversible actions.

problem: Minor: the value bias holds for long fixations only (short fixations show none), and the rising fixation duration over time held for problems B and C (no interaction).
Minor: Spiridonov et al. found a few exceptions (VR interactive sticks about +6 points, and interactivity helped problem A while hurting B and C), which fits 'not reliably'.

Minor: the false hints in Ammalainen and Moroshkina were unreportable (flashed) words and the effect is small; 'fixation' is the note's interpretation, and the nine-dot comparison is dot-turn vs non-dot-turn training (N=64).
Minor: NazoNazo 17.6% is the reasoning-model average on the 120-item subset (non-reasoning 7.6%), and BrainTeaser 53/63% is the best model (ChatGPT) on its two subtasks.

Mizumoto et al. call verification failure a distinctive failure mode that is only 5.23% to 39.34% of incorrect answers (4 models with usable logs), so most wrong answers do not contain the gold answer and it is not shown to be the main failure; the o1-like 70% figure (Wang et al.) is from math/science sets, not riddles.
fix: A distinctive reasoning-model failure on insight-like riddles is verification failure: a correct candidate appears in the thought log but is not endorsed (5.2% to 39.3% of wrong answers across four models with usable logs). Outside riddles, more than 70% of wrong o1-like responses on math and science sets contain at least one correct thought (Wang et al.), and hidden states encode intermediate-answer correctness (ROC-AUC above 0.7 in-distribution, Zhang et al.), so models may know more than they endorse.

problem: Minor: the 'Oh!' evidence is a qualitative thought-log observation in Mizumoto v1 (Claude Opus 4 and Grok 4 only, absent from the later arXiv version I opened); d'Aliberti's own shift annotation shows shifted traces were better in crosswords.

Minor: step-back alone on TimeQA is 41.5 to 66.0 (+24.5; the paper's 27% includes retrieval), physics and chemistry gains are +6.8 and +10.9, and structure-matched examples (RISCORE) were tested on multiple-choice riddles with smaller gains.

Numbers check out (six-coin 10/48 vs ten-coin 36/48 within 5 min, z=2.67, p=.008; partial-ring 4/27 vs straight-line 11/27, chi2=4.52; Ormerod et al. 2002 abstract confirms the eight-coin effect), but all three sources are the same Lancaster group (Ormerod, Chronicle, MacGregor), so the generalisation rests on one lab.

Sources report minimal or modest (non-significant) gains from visual or 'go outside' hints rather than none, and large gains came from combined aids and training (Kershaw and Ohlsson; Chein et al. got 46% with training plus a partial-solution hint), not from partial-solution hints alone.
fix: Hints that only say to go outside the box, or give visual cues, give little or no gain on the nine-dot problem (base rate under 5% in a few minutes; shading cue minimal gain, verbal plus visual hints slight gain). Large gains came only when aids addressing several difficulties were combined, for example training plus a hint that gives away part of the solution (46% solved in Chein et al.).

problem: Jones (2003) found that all 30 solvers had an impasse (fixation time at or above personal mean plus 2 SD on some move) somewhere before the taxi move, only 5 immediately before, and all 7 non-solvers also had at least one impasse; it did not show that the longest fixation precedes the key move in every solver (only that the taxi move had longer average fixation than the 3 moves before and after, p<.01). Fedor et al. (2017) do name inactivity and repeated attempts as behavioural correlates of impasse.
fix: Impasse is observable in behaviour: in a car-park insight problem (Jones 2003, N=37 analysable) all 30 solvers showed an impasse, defined as a move fixation time at or above that person's mean plus 2 SD, before the key taxi move (5 immediately before it), and fixation time on the taxi move was longer than on the three moves before and after it; non-solvers also had impasses. A neural model paper (Fedor et al. 2017) cites inactivity and repeated attempts as behavioural correlates of impasse.

problem: Wang et al. (2026): 7 of 11 deployments follow the reporting duty (93.2-100%) and 4 only 0.6-10.1%, but the 90.6-99.4% pre-action and 5.8-11.5% mid-task figures are for just gpt-4.1 and gpt-5.5; other compliant deployments (gemini-3.8-flash, gpt-6-astra, claude-opus-5) hold 74-100% mid-task and fail instead at completion (48-64%), so the mid-task failure is not general.

(2026, tau2-bench telecom): 7 of 11 models follow a progress-reporting duty on 93.2-100% of checkpoints and 4 on only 0.6-10.1%; for gpt-4.1 and gpt-5.5 reports are correct at 90.6-99.4% of pre-action checkpoints and 87.3-88.9% after completion but only 5.8-11.5% mid-task, while several newer models are accurate mid-task (74-100%) and weak at completion (48-64%), so the weak stage varies by model.

problem: Li et al. check out (verbal confidence AUROC 0.85 at completion, none above 0.60 at 50% progress), but in d'Aliberti and Ribeiro the pooled OR 0.77 (CI 0.58-1.02, p=0.070, N=723,200) is the association between entropy and whether a shift occurs, not entropy predicting when a shift helps.
fix: Uncertainty signals (verbal confidence, perplexity, entropy, consistency) predict failure well only at the end of a long-horizon agent trajectory (verbal confidence mean AUROC 0.85 at completion over 15 model-benchmark pairs) and poorly mid-way (no signal above mean AUROC 0.60 at 50% progress). In reasoning traces, token entropy was only weakly and inconsistently associated with whether a spontaneous shift occurs (pooled OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.02, p=0.070, N=723,200; positive in crosswords, negative in math).

fix: Reflection or a forced re-check after the first answer mostly confirms it. In 8 reasoning models on 5 maths sets over 90% of reflections are confirmatory, wrong-to-right is under about 2%, first-candidate accuracy is within 1.4-3.5 points of final, and reflections take 16.8-47.8% of tokens. Without an outside label, prompted self-correction lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round, 41.8 after two); with an oracle stop it raises it (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5). The paired right-to-wrong rate for a forced Wait is still unreported.

problem: The 32.2->40.6 math gain (d'Aliberti Table 5, probably Qwen2.5-1.5B) is for a reconsideration cue appended to all prompts, not only high-entropy ones (entropy gating is a separate appendix analysis with larger gains); shifts are 'strongly harmful' on math and only 'mildly harmful' on crosswords. 6.31%, 85-95%, AUC>0.7 and >0.9 on AIME at 32B are confirmed.
fix: Spontaneous self-verification by RL-trained reasoning models rarely finds errors. Mid-trace shifts occur in 6.31% of traces and are harmful on math (strongly) and mildly so on crosswords; about 85 to 95% of rechecks in Qwen3-8B are confirmatory; but appending a forced reconsideration cue to every prompt lifted math accuracy from 32.2% to 40.6% (small Qwen2.5 model), with gains larger on high-entropy instances. Hidden states carry a correctness signal (probe ROC-AUC above 0.7, above 0.9 on AIME for the 32B distill) that the model does not use.

arXiv 1207.5879 and 1408.2048 are the same paper (Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony, Selecting Computations) and the MITECS overview is by Russell, a co-author; Theorem 7 and the myopic-stops-too-early point are verified in that single source.
fix: The ideal rule from rational metareasoning (stop when no available computation has expected value above its cost) is intractable in general. Per Hay, Russell, Tolpin and Shimony (2012; a single source), cheap myopic or blinkered approximations exist, and the optimal policy computes whenever the myopic one does (Theorem 7), so myopic rules often stop too early where one step is worth zero but several together pay.

Numbers verified, but Tyen et al. report that with the true error location 18 to 44 percent of originally wrong traces become correct, which is not 'most' wrong traces.

Telling the model the true error location lets it fix a substantial minority of wrong traces (+18 to +44 percent of wrong traces corrected, depending on task), but a random location breaks 7 to 16 percent of right traces.

problem: All numbers verified (TTS 60.0 to 73.3, 3.3 to 23.3; DIV-SE 15/23 to 97, GPT-3.5 Blocksworld no gain, LLaMA-2 ZS-CoT 31.32 to 32.00), but 'gains shrink as the base model gets stronger' holds only within TTS and is contradicted at the weak end by DIV-SE, where weaker models gain nothing.

Both use majority vote, not a verifier. In TTS the gain is smaller for the stronger GPT-4.1-mini than for GPT-4o-mini, but DIV-SE needs a model strong enough to follow the approach prompts.

Two independent groups. Both need model internals or an answer-probing call.
